pi.name: Monica Dus
pi.title: Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology; Assistant Vice President for Research (Natural Sciences and Engineering) and Director of the Office of National Laboratories
pi.bio: Monica Dus earned her Ph.D. in Molecular Biology from the Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory School of Biological Sciences in 2008. She is a Professor in the Department of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology at the University of Michigan and serves as Assistant Vice President for Research and inaugural Director of U-M's Office of National Laboratories. Her Laboratory of Molecular Nutrition studies the interplay between food, genes, and physiology, with a focus on nutrigenomics, nutrient sensing, and the effects of diet on the brain. She is a 2023 Guggenheim Fellow, a 2023-2024 White House Fellow, and a recipient of the NSF CAREER Award and NIH New Innovator Award.

lab_description: The Dus Laboratory of Molecular Nutrition views nutrients as more than energy and raw materials: they act as life's sensors, regulators, and actuators. The lab works across molecules, genes, cells, organs, and whole organisms to understand how nutrients guide biology, health, and disease. Its initial focus on how diet affects the brain has expanded to developmental and aging processes. Using Drosophila and rodent models, the lab has shown that sugar breakdown products silence genes required for taste cell function, that high-sugar diets desensitize brain circuits controlling appetite and food memory, and that these effects can be reversed by returning to lower-sugar diets. Current work addresses questions in precision nutrition, including optimal diets across life stages and the role of genetic variation.

research_areas.title: Nutrigenomics: how nutrients manipulate genetic switches
research_areas.summary: The lab discovered that nutrients and their metabolic byproducts can activate or silence genes, with particular impacts on brain function and health.

research_areas.title: Sugar's impact on taste perception
research_areas.summary: Sugar breakdown products silence genes essential for taste cell function, causing animals to lose sweetness sensitivity with increased consumption, which in turn alters food choices.

research_areas.title: Sugar's effects on brain regulation of eating
research_areas.summary: High sugar consumption desensitizes brain regions controlling appetite and disrupts dopamine signaling needed to form food memories important for satiety.

research_areas.title: Reversibility of dietary damage
research_areas.summary: Negative effects of high-sugar diets can be reversed by returning to lower-sugar options, suggesting taste buds and brains can be retrained toward healthier eating.

research_areas.title: Precision nutrition
research_areas.summary: Current investigations address optimal diets for different life stages, genetic factors in nutrition, and whether truly personalized nutrition is achievable.
